title: Is BERT Really Robust? A Strong Baseline for Natural Language Attack on Text Classification and Entailment
authors: Di Jin, Zhijing Jin, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Peter Szolovits

pages.title: Fooling BERT by Swapping a Few Words
pages.subtitle: Adversarial examples, but for text

blocks.html: Adversarial examples are easy to picture for images: add a sprinkle of invisible pixel noise and a panda becomes a gibbon, with no human able to see the change. Text refuses to play along. Words are discrete — there is no “tiny nudge” to a word, you either change it or you do not — and any change is, by definition, visible to a reader. So the bar is higher: you must alter a sentence enough to flip a classifier while a person still sees the same meaning, fluent grammar, and the same correct label.

TextFooler is a black-box attack that does exactly this against modern text models, including BERT. Black-box means it never touches the model’s weights or gradients — it only sends queries and reads back the output probabilities, the same access any user of a deployed API would have. That realism is the point: it is the threat a real-world attacker can actually mount.

Here is a concrete success from the paper, a movie-review sentiment classifier. Original (predicted positive): “their computer animated faces are very expressive.” TextFooler’s version (predicted negative): “their computer animated faces are very affective.” One word changed, the meaning preserved to a human — and the label flipped.

The recipe in one line: (1) find the few words that matter most to the prediction, then (2) replace them with meaning-preserving synonyms — constrained by part-of-speech and sentence-level semantic similarity — until the label flips while the sentence stays grammatical and faithful.

The answer to the title’s question turns out to be a resounding no: BERT’s accuracy can be driven from the high 80s/90s down to the low teens or single digits by changing only a small fraction of words per sentence.

Changing every word would obviously wreck the sentence and destroy its meaning. So TextFooler first asks a sharp question: which words actually drive the model’s decision? Most words in a sentence are filler the classifier barely uses; a few carry almost all the weight. Find those, and you can flip the prediction with the fewest possible edits — which also keeps the sentence closest to the original.
The probe is simple: delete each word in turn and measure how much the model’s confidence in the correct label drops. A large drop means that word was load-bearing.

Term by term: $I_{w_i}$ is the importance score of word $w_i$; $F_y(X)$ is the model’s predicted probability for the true label $y$ on the full sentence $X$; and $F_y(X_{\setminus w_i})$ is that same probability after deleting word $w_i$. The difference is how much removing $w_i$ hurts the model’s confidence in $y$. (When deletion actually changes the predicted label, the paper uses a slightly richer score that also credits the size of the new class’s confidence.) The bigger $I_{w_i}$, the more the model leans on that word.

Words are sorted by importance, stop-words are skipped (swapping “the” helps nobody), and the attack targets the highest-impact words first. In the sentiment example above, “expressive” scores high because it is precisely the word telling the model the review is positive — so it is attacked first.

pages.title: Step 2 — Find Safe Synonyms
pages.subtitle: Replace the meaning's carrier, not the message

blocks.html: For each important word, TextFooler gathers candidate replacements and runs them through a gauntlet of constraints so the swap stays invisible to a human reader. A replacement only survives if it passes all three:

items: Synonym extraction. Take the $N$ nearest neighbors of the word in a counter-fitted word-embedding space. Plain word embeddings notoriously place “good” and “bad” close together (they appear in similar contexts); counter-fitting post-processes the vectors so true synonyms pull together and antonyms push apart — avoiding the disaster of swapping a word for its opposite.
Part-of-speech match. Keep only candidates with the same POS as the original (verb→verb, noun→noun, adjective→adjective), so the sentence stays grammatical.

Semantic-similarity check. Encode the original sentence and the candidate-edited sentence with the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) and keep the swap only if the cosine similarity of the two sentence embeddings stays above a threshold $\tau$ — a guard on sentence-level meaning, not just word-level.

blocks.html: Reading it: a candidate replacement $c$ is accepted only if the resulting adversarial sentence $X_{\text{adv}}$ stays within USE similarity $\tau$ of the original $X$, and $c$ shares the part of speech of the word $w_i$ it replaces. These two guards are exactly what keep the output fluent and meaning-preserving rather than gibberish.

Among the candidates that survive all filters, the attacker picks the one that most reduces the model’s confidence in the correct label (or most pushes it toward a target label). “Expressive” → “affective” passes every check — same adjective POS, high sentence similarity, a dictionary near-synonym — yet it tips the classifier over to “negative.”

TextFooler is a greedy procedure (Algorithm 1 in the paper). It walks down the importance-ranked word list and, for each word, makes the best meaning-preserving swap available, checking after every change whether the label has flipped.

items: Rank all words by importance (Step 1) and drop stop-words.
Take the most important remaining word and build its filtered synonym candidate set (Step 2).
Among candidates passing the POS and USE-similarity constraints, choose the one that most hurts the true-label confidence.
If the prediction has now flipped, return the adversarial sentence; otherwise lock in this best swap and move to the next important word.
Stop when the label flips, or when the important words are exhausted (a failure for that sentence).

blocks.html: Why greedy rather than searching all combinations? Because the space of possible multi-word substitutions is astronomically large; greedy, importance-first editing finds a flip cheaply and tends to touch only a handful of words. And because the whole thing is purely query-based, it works on any text classifier behind an API — no gradients, no model internals — which is what makes it both a realistic black-box threat and a strong, reusable baseline for measuring NLP robustness.
The numbers are dramatic. Against BERT fine-tuned for text classification, TextFooler collapses accuracy across every dataset while perturbing only a small share of words:

Look at IMDB: BERT goes from 90.9% accurate to 13.6% by changing just 6.1% of the words — and IMDB reviews average around 215 words, so that is roughly a dozen synonym swaps in a long paragraph. On the textual-entailment task SNLI, BERT’s accuracy falls from about 89 to roughly 4, with only a few words changed because the sentences are short.

The same attack flattens the other architectures too — WordCNN and WordLSTM classifiers drop to single digits as well — so the brittleness is not a quirk of BERT alone. But the headline is that the supposedly robust, heavily pretrained transformer is no more durable than a humble CNN against meaning-preserving word substitution. The answer to “Is BERT really robust?” is plainly no.

pages.title: Did the Meaning Survive? Human Validation
pages.subtitle: The model is fooled but a person is not

blocks.html: An attack on text is only meaningful if humans still read the adversarial sentence as the same content with the same label — otherwise it is just a typo or gibberish, which fools no one and proves nothing. The authors back this up with three human studies, on grammaticality, meaning preservation, and human label agreement.

The results hold up: human judges rate the perturbed sentences as nearly as grammatical as the originals (e.g. about 4.2 vs 4.0 out of 5 on MR), and human annotators continue to assign the original (correct) label to the adversarial sentences the large majority of the time. Sentence-level semantic similarity to the original stays high (the USE constraint enforces it). In short, people barely notice the edit, while the model flips completely.

The threat is genuine: the model is fooled, but a human is not. That gap — the exact opposite of a typo attack that confuses humans too — is what makes synonym substitution a legitimate adversarial example for NLP.

The paper also shows the adversarial sentences transfer across models (a flip crafted on one classifier often fools another) and that adversarial training on TextFooler-generated examples partially hardens the model — the standard attack/defense loop. TextFooler became a de-facto standard baseline and stress test, motivating defenses such as certified word-substitution robustness and prompting a broad reckoning with just how fragile large language models are to word-level changes that humans hardly register.
